newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BHP interested in Arco Australia assets.
newsitem.headline: BHP interested in Arco Australia assets.

text.p: The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd said on Thursday it would assess the Australian coal assets of Atlantic Richfield Co (ARCO) with a view to a possible purchase of Arco's coal mines in north Queensland.

BHP Australia Coal spokesman Ian Dymock said the assessment followed Arco Coal's announcement on Wednesday that it was evaluating the likely withdrawal from its coal mining operations in Australia and the United States.
"Like all these properties that come up for sale from time to time, we will be making an assessment. We would not discount it," Dymock told Reuters.
Arco's Australian investments include joint venture interests in the Blair Athol, Gordonstone and Curragh coal mines in Queensland's Bowen Basin.
Dymock said the Gordonstone mine, a three million tonne-a-year coking coal operation and Curragh, producing 2.5 million tonnes annually of thermal coal, were adjacent to BHP Coal's Crinum mine.
With start-up costs for new coal mines of about A$400 million, BHP would assess the two mines' viability, Dymock said.
Arco's three coal mines produce about 20 million tonnes, representing about 20 percent of Queensland's total production.
RTZ Plc-CRA Ltd is Arco's joint venture partner in the Blair Athol mine as well as the undeveloped Clermont project and has pre-emptive rights over these properties.
Arco Coal Australia president Bill Wagener said the overall process of its coal business review was expected to take at least six months and could extend into 1998.
"While Arco has some of the best coal assets in the world, we no longer regard them as part of our core business," Arco chairman and chief executive Mike Bowlin said in a statement.
Arco would be likely either to monetise its Australian coal interests through a public offering in the Australian equity markets or an outright sale, he said.
Bowlin said his group believed the United States business had achieved critical mass.
In the United States where Arco was the fourth-largest coal producer, a stand-alone company would be formed from Arco's mining operations in Wyoming, Colorado and Utah.
As part of the review, Arco would investigate spinning off the new United States company to existing Arco shareholders, as well as other alternatives, Bowlin said.
Net income from coal operations in the 1996 year fell to US$60 million from US$75 million in 1995.
Coal assets at the 1996 year-end totalled US$1.75 billion with employment at 2,600 including about 1,000 in Australia.
